title: Work Well With Others
objective: Complete a real project task with others, agree and fulfil your own role, and use evidence to explain how you worked together.

blocks.text: GROW · Art · Week 6. Trinity Arts Award Silver. Work Well With Others.
Objective: Complete a real project task with others, agree and fulfil your own role, and use evidence to explain how you worked together.
Success evidence: an actual team task, the pupil’s agreed contribution, a real exchange and response, and a precise link to earlier collaboration records.
Unit 2 is your arts leadership project. Keep it distinct from your personal arts challenge in Unit 1. These lessons support your real project at its planned scale.
40-minute lesson frame. Real activity may continue in recorded programme time. No event, attendance or booking is asserted here.

This deck directly serves Silver Unit 2, Arts leadership, Parts 2D. Part 2D requires working effectively with others. Preserve the pupil’s own contribution, actual exchanges and response to collaborators. Source: tools/artsaward/SPEC.json, Silver and universal rules. Silver has TWO units, evidenced separately: Unit 1 Arts practice and pathways; Unit 2 Arts leadership. Mark P / A / N per part. ONE Attempted is allowed PER UNIT. Any Not Attempted = Below Pass. Results are Pass / Below Pass only. The whole Silver portfolio has a 20-file cap across both units, not twenty per unit. Organise evidence by unit and part. Nine cumulative part files or two clearly sectioned unit files are optional layouts. Name the actual file plus page, slide or timecode for each item. One real record may support two parts with clear locators; do not count duplicate copies as extra evidence. The four assessment areas are art form knowledge and understanding, creativity, planning and review, and communication. Only an adviser trained at Silver may assess; delivery is through a validated centre. Confirm these locally, not as an accomplished fact in this deck. Adults may scribe exact pupil words or confirmed signs and check them back, but must not write the pupil’s plan, review or evidence. Staff may separately record factual observations. Core, Extend and Challenge are support choices within Silver and retain the actual role, contribution and evidence. No public showing is imposed as a Silver requirement. Fourteen forty-minute sessions do not supply all 95 programme hours; record actual further guided and independent time.

Identify a genuine remaining team task or necessary project follow-up with the pupil: for example completing an agreed display label, returning shared resources, checking a project record with its contributors or passing on collected feedback. The task must relate to the real arts project, with willing collaborators and a meaningful pupil role. Do not stage a dispute or a second public event to manufacture evidence. Prepare blank paper and two simple teacher-made art images for the model. One may show dots and curves, with the caption Dots and curves written before testing readability. A hypothetical disagreement may teach a method; only actual working with others supplies the pupil’s 2D activity evidence. Retrieve earlier 2B/2C collaboration records to connect, not replace, the new real task. If no collaborator is available, label any rehearsal honestly and arrange an appropriate opportunity.

stages.title: Arrival · retrieve
stages.data-ta1: Prepare actual records and a needed task. Missing evidence prompts retrieval or genuine work, never an invented past contribution.

blocks.text: Bring a real project test or delivery record. Find your own action and another person’s contribution.
Choose a needed team task with a clear result: checking a caption, returning tools or sharing feedback. Ask who is involved and what each can do.
Agree a collaborator, who may be a staff member. Keep your role clear when receiving reading, movement or equipment support.

stages.title: Starter · create the need
stages.data-ta1: Present the case as a fictional teaching example. Do not invite pupils to name classmates as difficult people or disclose private conflicts.

blocks.text: Read this teaching case. Two people are finishing a small art display. One wants a large caption so visitors can read it. The other wants the image to stay in full view.
Both are thinking about access to the art. Their ideas differ, but neither needs to be treated as a personal attack. What could they try together before deciding?
Working well with others is more than saying we all got on. It includes hearing a point, agreeing an action, keeping a commitment and checking the result.

A calm team does not need to create an argument to show these skills. You can demonstrate useful cooperation when everyone agrees. The evidence comes from what you do with other people, not how dramatic the story sounds.

stages.title: I Do · model
stages.data-ta1: Make a real small display trial with a willing partner. Use actual responses and do not script an artificial disagreement.

blocks.text: Watch the adult test a display choice with a willing partner. They use two teacher-made images. First they write a short caption accurately naming a feature of one image. They ask what the partner needs to see or read clearly.
They listen without interrupting, then check the meaning: You want room around the image, and a caption you can read from here. Have I understood? The partner can correct that summary.
The adult offers a practical option: put the caption below the image rather than over its edge. They ask what the partner thinks and try the layout with loose pieces.
They agree their roles before fixing anything. In the model, the adult can position the image while the partner places the caption. Each confirms the job they are taking on.

Both do their part and then check the display together. They look from the actual viewing place and say what still needs attention. Agreement is tested against the result, not treated as the end of the work.
The adult records the real exchange from this model. Your team may agree another method. Do not copy the example as if it happened in your own project.

blocks.title: Work together towards a real result
blocks.caption: An agreement matters when people act on it.
blocks.alt: Work together towards a real result. LISTEN check the other view. AGREE name roles and action. DO fulfil your own part. CHECK look at the result together. An agreement matters when people act on it.

stages.title: We Do · everyone commits
stages.data-ta1: Read the actual prompt and choices; support the pupil to commit before checking. Use the item feedback as a model reason, not a judgement on personal taste. Keep real trials, meetings, views and project actions separate from these teaching examples.

data.heading: Order a shared display task
data.instruction: Put this agreed small display task in order. Use each place once. Hear both views before assigning or fixing the pieces.

items.label: Each person carries out the part they agreed.
items.feedback: Do your own part and tell the collaborator if something changes.

items.label: Check the display together from the actual viewing place.
items.feedback: Agreement is checked against the result. Name any remaining action.

items.label: Hear both views and check what the collaborator means.
items.feedback: Listening gives the agreement a real basis; do not write someone’s reply in advance.

items.label: Agree who places the image, who places the caption and what support is needed.
items.feedback: Responsibilities need agreement. A shared task should still make each person’s contribution identifiable.

data.discussion: Carry out your real project task with your collaborator. Ask before changing their work, keep your own contribution clear and link it to an earlier example of teamwork.

stages.title: I Do 2 · connect
stages.data-ta1: Use the actual demonstration to show separate contributions. Help locate earlier real examples; do not add a pupil interpretation they have not given.

blocks.text: A finished display alone cannot show your contribution. Name your agreed task, action and joint check.
In the model, record who placed the image and caption, and the exchange that shaped the layout.
Explain your reasons. Keep other people’s words unchanged; check shared facts together.
Connect this task to a real earlier preparation or delivery example of listening, explaining or agreeing roles.
A shared record must identify each pupil’s contribution. An observer describes actions; your words, signs or confirmed choices supply your meaning.
Locate both examples under Unit 2, Part 2D for your later review.

blocks.title: A group statement and an identifiable contribution
blocks.caption: Use your actual task, not the model’s story.
blocks.alt: A group statement and an identifiable contribution. TOO BROAD we finished together no individual action shown. CLEARER RECORD my agreed role and action a real response and check. Use your actual task, not the model’s story.

stages.title: We Do 2 · lab
stages.data-ta1: This is real project collaboration, not a role-play. Support communication and realistic role choices while leaving the decision with the pupil and collaborator.

blocks.text: With your real collaborator, choose the next small step in your project task. Explain what you think is needed, then ask for their view. Wait long enough for them to answer in their usual way.
Check that you understand any different suggestion. Point to the materials, record or space if this helps. You can disagree about a method while respecting the person.
Agree who does what and what support each person needs. Make the action small enough to carry out and check in the available time. Keep a brief note of the agreement before acting.
If there is a safety issue or an unresolved problem beyond your role, pause and involve the responsible adult. Do not turn a peer agreement into permission to ignore a risk.

stages.title: Independent · evidence
stages.data-ta1: Keep actual work and checking central. Scribe exact words or confirmed signs, check them back and preserve factual observations separately.

blocks.text: Carry out your agreed part of the actual project task. Keep the purpose in view. Use the support you agreed without giving away the decisions that belong to your role.
Stay in contact with your collaborator as the work develops. Tell them if something changes or you need more time. Ask before changing their contribution, and check any new action together.

Core: use a short role prompt and access help. Take your own part in the real task, hear the collaborator’s view, agree an action and check the result together. Show or dictate your exact contribution for the record.
Extend: fulfil your agreed role, record the real exchange and explain how you responded. Link the new task to an earlier example of working with others in the project.

Challenge: keep the same actual task, individual contribution and evidence. Compare how you worked together now with an earlier moment, and use a real response to explain a useful change in your approach.

When the task is ready, check the result with the people involved. Did it do the job you agreed? Name a remaining action honestly if it did not. A cooperative exchange does not require a perfect outcome.

Record your role, action, response and result in Unit 2, Part 2D. Name the actual file and page, slide or timecode for this task and the earlier example. Do not present a fictional case or an absent collaborator as real evidence.

stages.title: Exit · confirm the shared result
stages.data-ta1: Verify actual locators and individual contributions. The next review must use real evidence, not a general claim that teamwork went well.

blocks.text: Show your collaborator the record of the agreed task. Check the factual details: who did which part, what changed and what the result was. Keep each person’s view clear where the views differ.
Point to one thing you personally contributed. Then acknowledge a real contribution from another person. This does not reduce your role; it makes the account more accurate.

Use the saved locations to find both today’s task and your earlier project example. These records can support your own leadership review next week. Keep unfinished work named so the review does not turn a plan into a claim of completion.

print.intro: Complete a needed project task with real collaborators. Keep your own contribution and the actual exchange, then link it to earlier work with others.
focusRows: What task did we agree, and what was my own role?
What did I do, what did the collaborator contribute, and how did we respond?
What result did we check together, and which earlier record helps explain my approach?
tiers: Core: use a short role prompt and access help. Take your own part in the real task, hear the collaborator’s view, agree an action and check the result together. Show or dictate your exact contribution for the record.
Extend: fulfil your agreed role, record the real exchange and explain how you responded. Link the new task to an earlier example of working with others in the project.

Challenge: keep the same actual task, individual contribution and evidence. Compare how you worked together now with an earlier moment, and use a real response to explain a useful change in your approach.
checks: The task and collaborators are real; the fictional teaching case is not treated as pupil evidence.
My own agreed role and actual contribution are identifiable.
The record preserves listening, agreement, action and a check with others.
A genuine earlier project example is linked without inventing a past action or response.
Unit 2 Part 2D records have actual file-plus-page, slide or timecode locators.
